questions.q: Why is a spot instance a reasonable choice for a job cluster but risky for an actively-used all-purpose cluster?
options: Job clusters can retry lost tasks automatically on fault-tolerant batch work, while reclaiming a spot instance mid-session interrupts a live user
Spot instances are only available on job clusters, never on all-purpose clusters
All-purpose clusters cannot run on any cloud provider's spot pricing tier
Spot instances always cost more than on-demand instances
questions.explain: The discount is the same either way — the difference is whether an interruption is a retried background task or a disrupted live session.

options: An idle all-purpose cluster nobody's using continuing to bill for compute it isn't running
A job cluster running out of local disk space
A skewed shuffle partition slowing down a query
A secret being hardcoded into notebook code
questions.explain: Without a configured auto-termination window, a cluster left open after someone steps away keeps billing for the rest of the day, running nothing.

questions.q: What does right-sizing mean, as opposed to over-provisioning 'just in case'?
options: Sizing a cluster to the workload's actual measured shape and real observed load, rather than padding for comfort
Always choosing the smallest instance type regardless of the job
Disabling autoscaling entirely
Running every job on a single shared cluster
questions.explain: Right-sizing uses the workload-shape analysis from Lesson 25 and real load numbers instead of an oversized guess.

questions.q: Why doesn't a 3x larger cluster necessarily run a job 3x faster?
options: A job's actual bottleneck (such as a skewed partition) may not benefit from additional compute at all, so extra size just adds cost without proportional speedup
Larger clusters always run every job slower
Cluster size has no effect on cost, only on speed
Databricks caps the maximum cluster size at 3x any job's minimum requirement
questions.explain: Lesson 25 covered exactly this: a bottleneck like a skewed partition doesn't scale away with more nodes, so over-provisioning just costs more for the same result.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does Chapter 5, 'Performance at Scale,' cover in total?
options: Photon's vectorized engine, AQE's runtime re-optimization, caching layers, cluster sizing by workload shape, and cost optimization
Only cluster autoscaling configuration
Row-level and column-level security in Unity Catalog
Delta Sharing's open protocol
questions.explain: Chapter 5 runs from Lesson 22 (Photon) through Lesson 26 (cost optimization); Chapter 6 covers security and governance next.
